Since Parser depends on other classes (TreeBuilder, HtmlTreeBuilder, XmlTreeBuilder, Document, Element, Node, ParseErrorList, ParseError, ParseSettings, Tokeniser, CharacterReader). We don't have implementations; for unit testing we can use mocks (e.g., Mockito) to simulate behavior. Since we need comprehensive tests, we can test: - constructor sets default settings from treeBuilder. - getTreeBuilder returns set builder. - setTreeBuilder returns parser and updates builder. - isTrackErrors based on maxErrors. - setTrackErrors updates maxErrors and returns parser. - getErrors returns errors after parseInput; we need to simulate parseInput using mock TreeBuilder that records parameters and returns a Document. - settings() getter and settings(ParseSettings) setter. - static parse creates HtmlTreeBuilder, parse called correctly. - parseFragment static methods. - parseXmlFragment. - parseBodyFragment: builds shell doc, uses parseFragment, ensures proper nodes appended; we can mock HtmlTreeBuilder to return list of nodes; but parseBodyFragment uses static method parseFragment which constructs new HtmlTreeBuilder inside; we can’t easily inject mock. Could use a real simple HTML fragment and verify behavior using Jsoup library? However we may not have actual Jsoup dependencies, but we can include them as test dependencies. In typical environment, Jsoup is present. The test can use real Jsoup to parse simple HTML and verify that body contains expected elements. - unescapeEntities: uses Tokeniser; we can test that it returns correct unescaped string using known entity e.g., "&" => "&". Use real Tokeniser from Jsoup. - parseBodyFragmentRelaxed delegates to parse. - htmlParser and xmlParser return Parser with appropriate TreeBuilder type; we can check instanceof. Thus we need to import org.jsoup.parser.*, org.jsoup.nodes.*. We'll write test class with multiple test methods. We'll use @Test annotation and assert statements. For mocking, we can use Mockito (add import). We'll create mock TreeBuilder that returns a mock Document, and set errors list. Implement testParseInputString: setTrackErrors(2), mock builder parse returns doc, verify errors tracking used. But we need to inject mock TreeBuilder into Parser via constructor. Parser constructor takes TreeBuilder; we can pass mock. We also need to stub builder.defaultSettings() to return new ParseSettings() maybe. Since ParseSettings is a class, we can use real instance. We also need to stub builder.parse method; method signature: parse(Reader, String, ParseErrorList, ParseSettings) returns Document. We'll use when(mockBuilder.parse(any(Reader.class), eq(baseUri), any(ParseErrorList.class), any(ParseSettings.class))).thenReturn(mockDoc); Also stub defaultSettings(). Test that after parseInput, parser.getErrors() returns appropriate list (tracking or not). For tracking, we need to capture the ParseErrorList passed; we can use ArgumentCaptor. Simplify: test that isTrackErrors influences errors list type: when maxErrors >0, errors is instance of ParseErrorList and tracking; but we can't inspect internal; we can verify that builder.parse received a ParseErrorList that is tracking (ParseErrorList.tracking returns list with tracking flag). We can inspect using reflection to check if list.isTrackErrors? Not known API. Safer: verify that errors returned by parser.getErrors() is same as the list passed to builder.parse (we can capture). " and verify doc.body() has child div. Test unescapeEntities: string "Tom & Jerry" -> "Tom & Jerry". Also test attribute mode maybe. Test parseBodyFragmentRelaxed: verify same as Parser.parse.
